patient_actor_hidden.History: The patient experienced sudden loss of consciousness while pitching in a baseball game. No history of trauma associated with the event. The patient regained consciousness after receiving cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
patient_actor_hidden.Social_History: Active, with regular participation in sports. No use of tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs reported.
patient_actor_hidden.Review_of_Systems: Negative for headaches, seizures, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, or dizziness prior to the event.

questions: While it was happening, did he have any convulsive movements or tongue biting, or did he wake up confused afterward?
Did he have any warning signs right before the episode (e.g., lightheadedness, sweating, nausea, blurred vision, or the sense of “about to faint”)?
Did he lose consciousness while sitting/lying down or while standing up (and was there any clear trigger like pain, coughing, urination, or straining)?
After the episode, did he have any chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath?
During the episode, did anyone notice his breathing pattern (e.g., normal vs gasping) and whether his eyes were rolled back or fixed?
How long was the loss of consciousness (in seconds/minutes), and did they fully return to normal immediately afterward?
What do the abdominal bumps look like in detail (e.g., red vs skin-colored, flat vs raised, itchy vs painful, any crusting/peeling, and how long have they been present)?
Are the papules located anywhere specific (e.g., face/scalp, trunk/abdomen, arms/legs, in skin folds) and do they have a central umbilication or crust?
Are the bumps present in clusters that have spread over time, and do any have a visible central “dimple” you could express cheesy material from if gently squeezed?
Has anyone noticed any fever, rapid worsening, or significant swelling of the lymph nodes (neck/armpit/groin) since the skin bumps started?
answers: “No, there weren’t any convulsive movements or tongue biting. She didn’t wake up confused afterward and seemed totally like herself.”

“I think she was just sitting and lying down when we noticed it—there wasn’t any standing up, pain, coughing, urination, or straining involved. She didn’t seem to lose consciousness; she acted normal the whole time.”
